candidates.title: LiberNovo’s motorized office chair reclines to 160 degrees, has seat cooling, and is up to 42% discount
candidates.full_text:
In 1976, two designers gave the office a chair that moved when you did. The Met calls Emilio Ambasz and Giancarlo Piretti’s Vertebra the first automatically adjustable office chair. Fifty years later, plenty of us still tug knobs and crank levers like we’re docking a spaceship. LiberNovo’s Maxis picks up that old idea and sizes it for bigger frames. Its Black Friday sale opens November 19, with up to 42% off in the US.

The Maxis is LiberNovo’s first line built from the ground up for big and tall users, rated to 399 lbs (181 kg) and certified to BIFMA X5.11, and fitted for people between 5’10” and 6’7″ (178 to 200 cm). Instead of scaling up a standard chair, LiberNovo resized the parts that tend to fail on larger bodies, from the seat depth to the headrest travel. It comes in three versions: Manual, Electric, and Airflow. List prices run $1,299, $1,799, and $1,859, which makes for one big leap and one tiny hop. Let’s walk the staircase one step at a time.

Click Here to Buy Now: Black Friday Deals End Soon!

All three versions of the Maxis share the same big-body frame. The seat is 20.5 inches (52 cm) deep, with a multi-density cushion that runs firmer at the rear and softer at the front edge, where the backs of your thighs rest. The backrest spans 16.9 inches at the shoulders and flares to 20.5 inches at the waist. The U-shaped headrest travels 5.5 inches up and down and 4.7 inches in and out. Arc-shaped armrests open from 15.7 to 23.6 inches wide, so they don’t crowd your waist.

Lean back in a Maxis and the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat all move together, a many-jointed cousin of the Vertebra’s idea. The eight-panel backrest flexes on 14 dual-link points and 16 ball joints. Six springs engage progressively by angle and weight, which LiberNovo says keeps the recline smooth under a heavier load. Five stops run from 105 degrees (Deep Focus) to 160 degrees (Spine Flow), and LiberNovo suggests 115 to 125 degrees for most of the day. Do the four-step setup once, and LiberNovo says you’ll rarely touch the controls again.

The Manual keeps lumbar support on a dial, with no motor and no battery, which suits anyone who wants a chair that never needs charging. The Electric swaps that dial for the ErgoPulse motor and carries a 2,200 mAh battery. The motor moves the lumbar zone in or out until it meets your lower back, forming an S-curve, so there’s no reaching behind you to twist a knob. Lumbar is step one of the Maxis setup, so you’ll feel this feature on day one. That’s the first half of what the extra $500 buys.

OmniStretch is the other half, a five-minute motorized stretch sequence that runs while you’re in deep recline. Both the Electric and the Airflow include it, and the Manual skips it. LiberNovo describes it as an in-chair stretch and reset, which makes it a handy pause between long work sessions and the walk to the kitchen. Whether it’s worth a share of $500 depends on how often you’d actually use it. If the honest answer is every afternoon, the math gets friendly fast.

The Airflow adds a seat fan to everything the Electric does. A 4,000 RPM centrifugal fan pulls air through a five-layer seat on two levels, and an occupancy sensor pauses it when you stand up, so it never spins for an empty chair. The battery grows from 2,200 to 3,000 mAh, and LiberNovo lists fan noise under 45 dB. The upholstery is Danish Gabriel Atlantic fabric, rated by its maker at more than 100,000 abrasion rubs. At list price, all of that sits $60 above the Electric, which is the easiest call on the page.

LiberNovo’s holiday sale opens November 19 and builds toward Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with up to 42% off in the US. Eligible purchases carry 30-day price protection, so buying early comes with a safety net for qualifying price changes. Every LiberNovo chair is backed by a 6-year frame warranty and a 2-year warranty on electronics. Orders unlock gift tiers by spending, topping out at a travel kit with an inflatable neck pillow, eye mask, and earplugs. US buyers can split the bill into four 0% Klarna payments. Fifty years after the Vertebra, the best pitch for a chair that moves with you is still the simplest: you stop thinking about it.

candidates.title: Kamen Rider’s 55th anniversary chronograph is limited to 1,971 pieces
candidates.full_text:
Fulton built the Kamen Rider anniversary watch around a single number: 1,971. That’s the year the show first aired, and it’s also how many of these chronographs exist. One per year, in a sense, and the run closes when the last one finds a wrist.

The watch is the Kamen Rider 55th Anniversary Special Chronograph, a radio-controlled solar chronograph from Direct Art Gallery (Dag) and the Swiss brand Fulton. It costs $313, reservations are open now through Dag’s shop, and the first watches ship in January 2027.

Fifty-five years have passed since the first Rider hit Japanese TV in 1971, and the watch is aimed squarely at the people who grew up in front of it. Dag says it plainly enough: this one goes to the adults who kept running with the show through the decades. The design carries that idea in every choice, starting with the two colors on the dial.

The dial runs a deep green with red accents, the two colors the release ties to the original Rider. A tachymeter-style bezel rings the dial with the words RIDER METER and a scale running 60 to 400.

The Rider crest sits at 12 o’clock, the Fulton name below it, and the words radio controlled solar chronograph printed small across the dial.

Three subdials sit across the face: a minute counter, a 24-hour dial, and a small-seconds dial at 6 o’clock cut like a turbine fan in red. It’s the liveliest detail on the watch, and anyone who knows the show will catch the reference before the second hand makes a lap. The pushers and crown sit at 2 and 4 o’clock, and the whole case reads chunky and confident, the way a tribute watch should.

The box holds two straps, and they change the watch completely. A heavy stainless bracelet gives it the everyday look, while a green cowhide strap with crimson stitching turns it into the fan piece. Dag includes a simple tool with the watch, so the swap happens at home in minutes, no trip to a watchmaker and no spring-bar fight.

Steel is the sensible default. The leather strap is the one you’ll reach for when someone asks about the watch, which they will, because the green dial with the red subdial doesn’t sit quietly on a wrist.

One watch, two personalities, and the swap takes minutes.

Inside, a radio-controlled solar movement does the two jobs every quartz owner hates doing. It listens for Japan’s standard time signal from the Otakadoya and Hagane transmitters, and the maker claims an accuracy of one second in 100,000 years from that signal, with the time correcting itself. Sunlight or room light feeds the solar cell, so there’s no battery to swap and no setting to fiddle with after a drawer month.

You never set it, and you never feed it a battery. That’s the whole maintenance schedule.

One thing to know before buying: the radio sync listens for Japan’s signal. The watch keeps time on its own anywhere, but the automatic correction is a Japan-at-home feature. Dag sells through its own shop, and the piece is built for the Japanese market.

Flip it over and the anniversary gets personal. The caseback carries the 55th anniversary logo in the same teal as the dial, and every watch gets its own serial number engraved beside it. The ring around the back is stamped with the facts: stainless steel, chronograph, and water resistance to 10 bar.

Read the logo closely and the joke lands. The anniversary mark prints 55TH GOGO!!, because go is the Japanese word for five, and the pun runs across the caseback, the presentation box, and the campaign art. It’s the kind of detail that separates a design made by fans from one made by a licensing department with a deadline.

Fulton isn’t a licensing shell. The Swiss brand started in Bienne in 1885, its Military model went into service in 1940, and its MEMO TIME alarm clock became a hit in 1954. Dag put the anniversary watch on that history, and it shows in the build: a real chronograph movement, a real steel case, and a design that treats the source with more care than a logo slap.

The box keeps the theme going. A green presentation case carries the 55th anniversary mark, and an original guarantee card comes with each numbered watch. It’s the paperwork a numbered edition should carry, and Dag didn’t skip it. Dag is also giving one away on X, a single winner picked from followers of its @direct_a_g account.

candidates.title: Antonia Tiny House Offers a Bedroom Without the Climb
candidates.full_text:
Loft bedrooms look efficient on paper. Move the bed upstairs, and suddenly there’s room for a proper kitchen or a sofa below. But that saved space comes with a compromise: stairs to navigate at night and a ceiling that may not let you stand upright. I’d rather have a little less cleverness in the floor plan and a bedroom I can simply walk into.

That’s the appeal of Antonia, an orderable modular home from Swedish company Vagabond Haven. Its main bedroom stays downstairs, while roughly 635 square feet across two levels leave room for a second sleeping area above. Two modules form an L around a terrace, giving the layout a useful bend rather than the proportions of a towable cabin. It’s designed to settle onto a foundation, delivered by truck and positioned by crane.

That bend in the floor plan does useful work. The living area occupies one wing, while the bedroom, bathroom, and stairs occupy the other. Between them, the terrace sits inside the L, reached through glass doors from both the living room and the downstairs bedroom. In the published renderings, outdoor seating makes this corner read as another place to spend time, not merely a landing outside the door. The images are illustrative, so finishes and details may change.

I like that the outdoor space has a clear relationship to the rooms around it. A deck can be generous and still feel detached from daily life if getting there means walking around the house. Here, the layout suggests an easy route from cooking dinner to eating outside. That’s a more convincing use of limited space than counting every square foot of decking as though it were another climate-controlled room.

Indoors, the kitchen and living room share a high ceiling because the loft stays over the opposite wing. The kitchen follows its own L-shaped plan, with a sink, cooktop, oven, and refrigerator/freezer in the illustrated furnished setup. A dishwasher is optional, and a four-seat dining table sits nearby. The proportions matter more to me than the styling: a table that can remain a table is preferable to furniture that needs a nightly transformation.

The material palette is restrained: vertical Thermopine siding outside, a steel-sheet roof, laminate flooring, and Forestia/Huntonit interior panels. White cabinetry and pale wood tones give the renderings a familiar cottage feel. More importantly, the ground-floor bedroom is shown with a double bed and fitted wardrobes, while the bathroom accommodates a shower, vanity, toilet, and washer/dryer. Those aren’t glamorous features. They’re the infrastructure that lets a small home function beyond a weekend.

Upstairs, the compromise is more visible. The loft rendering shows a second double bed, a desk, and seating beneath a low pitched ceiling, with stairs providing access. I’d see this as useful guest space or an occasional work retreat before making it the primary bedroom. Keeping the downstairs option means the house doesn’t ask everyone to accept the same relationship with stairs, headroom, and getting up at night.

Pricing needs the same practical reading. Vagabond Haven lists the unfurnished Antonia at €67,500 before VAT, with a €77,500 furnished example configuration. The base price isn’t the price of the staged interior: the company excludes items including heating, appliances, bathroom fittings, the terrace, delivery, and utility connections. Its stated delivery market is Europe, so these figures shouldn’t be mistaken for a ready-to-install U.S. offer. A beautiful rendering doesn’t make those additional decisions disappear.

I’d pay particular attention to where it lands. With so much glass facing the terrace, choosing what those windows overlook would be part of making this layout work. A view of trees and a view of a neighbor’s kitchen aren’t interchangeable. Antonia makes an appealing case for letting outdoor space shape a small home, but that makes its eventual setting just as important as what arrives on the truck.
